blocks.prompt: The Machine That Runs on You
blocks.text: A bicycle has no engine. It has no gas. It only has you. Your feet push the pedals. The pedals turn a chain. The chain turns the back wheel. The back wheel pushes against the ground, and you roll. When the bike leans one way, you turn the handlebars that same way. The bike comes back under you. That is how you stay up, and you do it without thinking. A bicycle wastes almost nothing. Nearly all of your pushing turns into rolling. That makes it the most useful machine anyone has ever built out of tubes and wire.

blocks.prompt: The Machine With No Pedals
blocks.text: The first bicycle had no pedals. In 1817, a German named Karl von Drais built a wooden machine with two wheels, one behind the other, and a bar to steer with. You sat on it and pushed the ground with your feet, like a scooter. People laughed at it. They also could not stop riding it. About fifty years later, someone bolted pedals straight onto the front wheel. Now your feet never touched the ground. But there was a problem. The pedals were fixed to the wheel, so one turn of your legs meant exactly one turn of the wheel. If you wanted to go faster, you needed a bigger wheel. So the wheels grew. And grew. By the 1870s the front wheel was nearly as tall as the rider, who sat up on top of it, a long way from the ground. Falling off hurt. Something had to change.

blocks.prompt: The Chain That Shrank the Wheel
blocks.text: For twenty years the fastest bicycle in the world was also the most dangerous. It was called the high wheeler, and it ran on one stubborn rule: the pedals were bolted straight onto the front wheel, so one turn of your legs carried you exactly the distance around that wheel. Speed meant size. By the 1880s the front wheel had grown to nearly five feet across, the rider sat above it, and a stone in the road could pitch him headfirst onto the ground. The fix was a chain. In 1885 an English maker named John Kemp Starley built a machine he called the Rover. It had two small wheels of equal size, a low seat, and a chain running back from the pedals to the rear wheel. The clever part was the sprockets, the toothed wheels the chain wraps around. A large sprocket at the pedals driving a small one at the hub means the back wheel spins several times for every single turn of your legs. You get the speed of a giant wheel without the giant wheel. People called it the safety bicycle, and within about ten years the high wheelers were gone. Three years after the Rover, John Boyd Dunlop wrapped bicycle wheels in tubes of air. Until then riders had rattled along on solid rubber. Pneumatic tires made the bicycle quieter, faster, and far more comfortable, and every car built since has copied the idea. Now look closely at the wheel itself. Those thin spokes are far too skinny to hold anything up by pushing. They are wires pulled tight, hauling the rim inward from every direction at once. The hub does not rest on the spokes underneath it. It hangs from the ones above. Your whole weight hangs from a few strands of steel wire, and you have never once thought about it.

notes: The gyroscope explanation is mostly wrong

blocks.prompt: How a Bicycle Really Stays Up
blocks.text: Ask most people how a bicycle stays up and they will say gyroscopes. A spinning wheel resists being tipped, the story goes, and that resistance holds the rider upright. It is a tidy explanation. It is also mostly wrong. In 2011 a team of engineers built a bicycle designed to kill the idea. Above each ordinary wheel they mounted a second wheel and spun it backward at the same speed, canceling the gyroscopic effect down to nothing. They also removed the trail, which is the small distance by which the front tire touches the ground behind the steering axis. Both of the classic explanations were now switched off. Then they gave the machine a push down a smooth floor with nobody on it. It rolled, wobbled, corrected itself, and carried on upright, exactly as an ordinary riderless bicycle does. Whatever holds a bicycle up, it does not need gyroscopes. Here is what actually happens. A bicycle stays up by falling and then steering out of the fall. Lean left, and the front wheel turns left, not because you decide it should but because the geometry and the weight of the front end make it happen on their own. The wheel tracks a curve underneath the falling body and catches it, the way your hand shoots sideways to stop a broom from tipping off your palm. Then the bike leans slightly the other way and the correction repeats. A moving bicycle is not balanced. It is falling continuously and steering out of it, hundreds of times a minute, and you never notice a single one. This is also why nobody can teach you to ride. The corrections are far too small and far too fast for words. Your body has to work them out by falling, which is the only reason training wheels are so useless: they hold you upright and stop you learning the exact thing you came to learn. And it is why the strangest fact about a bicycle is not that it is hard to learn. It is that it is impossible to forget.

blocks.prompt: Read the passage, then work through each part.

notes: Most efficient machine ever built for moving a body
A human on a bike beats the condor
1890s: the safety bicycle boom
Cyclists campaigned for paved roads before cars existed
The Wright brothers ran a bike shop in Dayton, Ohio
Bike shop skills built the 1903 Flyer

blocks.prompt: The Bicycle That Taught Us to Fly
blocks.text: There is a chart that engineers like to show. It plots how much energy it costs a creature to move its own body a given distance. The condor came out best of every animal measured. A human on foot did not do well at all, landing about a third of the way down the list, comfortably beaten by animals with far smaller brains. Then someone thought to measure a human on a bicycle, and the human on a bicycle beat the condor. It was not close. A well-built bicycle turns something like ninety percent of the work your legs do into forward motion, an efficiency no engine has ever approached. Steve Jobs read about that chart as a boy and never let it go. A computer, he liked to say, is a bicycle for our minds. The machine did not stay a toy for long. In the 1890s, once the safety bicycle was cheap enough for ordinary people, something happened that nobody had planned. For the first time a young woman could leave her own street without a horse, a carriage, a chaperone, or anybody's permission. She could simply go. Doctors invented an illness called bicycle face and warned her off. Newspapers mocked the loose trousers she wore in order to pedal. Susan B. Anthony, asked in 1896 what she made of the craze, answered: "I think it has done more to emancipate women than anything else in the world." She was not being poetic. She was describing a machine that made unsupervised distance cheap. The bicycle also built the roads. Through the 1880s and 1890s American cyclists organized themselves into the League of American Wheelmen and lobbied hard for something almost nobody else wanted yet: smooth, paved, publicly funded roads. They got them. When the first automobiles rolled out a few years later, they found a road network already waiting, campaigned for and paid for by people on bicycles. And then there is Dayton, Ohio. Two brothers ran a bicycle shop there. They repaired frames, laced wheels, built their own line of bikes, and in the process absorbed a lesson the aviation experts of the day had missed entirely. Every serious flying machine of the 1890s was designed to be inherently stable, to hold itself level the way a boat does. Orville and Wilbur Wright, who spent their working days fixing machines that stay up only because a person keeps correcting them, assumed the opposite. An aircraft, they decided, should be unstable and controllable, and the pilot should fly it the way a rider rides. That assumption, worked out over bicycle handlebars, is a large part of why their Flyer left the ground at Kitty Hawk in 1903 and their rivals' machines did not. The rest came out of the shop too: the wing-warping wires, the bicycle chains that drove the propellers, the wheel they mounted sideways on a bike to test airfoils by riding it down the street, the wind tunnel they built between repairs. The bicycle is a strange kind of ancestor. No single person invented it. Its basic shape has barely changed since 1890. It has no engine, no fuel, and no computer, and it is still, by a wide margin, the most efficient machine anyone has ever made. It carried the ball bearing, the chain drive, the pneumatic tire, and the tension-spoked wheel into the world, handed all four to the automobile, and then quietly got out of the way. It taught half the population that they could go wherever they liked. And it taught two brothers in Ohio that balance is not something you have. It is something you do.
